title: Third declension: consonant stems

objectives.can: Parse third-declension nouns with consonant stems and find the stem from the genitive.

explanation.summary: Many of the most important words of the New Testament, such as σάρξ, πνεῦμα, ὄνομα and χάρις, belong to the third declension. Their nominative singular is often hard to match with their other forms, so the skill to learn is to find the stem in the genitive and build the rest from it.

sections.heading: Stem plus ending
body: A first- or second-declension noun shows its stem in every form: λόγ-ος, λόγ-ου, λόγ-ῳ. A third-declension noun has a stem that ends in a consonant, and the endings are added directly to it. The nominative singular is where the stem is most likely to be hidden, because the consonant at the end of the stem may change or disappear when it meets the nominative ending or stands at the end of a word.

So lexica give the nominative and the genitive together, for example σάρξ, σαρκός. Remove the genitive ending -ος and what is left is the stem: σαρκ-. Every other form is built from that stem, and the genitive tells you which stem to use.

sections.heading: The endings
body: The usual endings of a masculine or feminine noun are given in the table. The accusative singular is -α after a consonant stem; a few nouns, such as χάρις, also have an accusative singular in -ν (χάριν), and the corpus attests both. The vocative is often like the nominative or like the bare stem.
Neuter nouns, like all neuters, have a nominative and accusative that are alike, and in the plural those two end in -α.

sections.heading: What happens to the final consonant
body: A stem that ends in κ, γ or χ combines with the nominative -ς to give ξ: σαρκ- gives σάρξ, and νυκτ- gives νύξ. A stem that ends in τ, δ or θ cannot stand before -ς and drops that consonant: χαριτ- gives χάρις, ἐλπιδ- gives ἐλπίς. The same drop happens before the dative plural -σι: ποδ- gives ποσίν, and the stem of οὖς, which is ὠτ-, gives ὠσίν.

Neuters in -μα (σῶμα, ὄνομα, αἷμα, στόμα, ῥῆμα, θέλημα) have the stem in -ματ-. A word cannot end in τ in Greek, so the nominative singular simply loses it: the stem σωματ- gives the nominative σῶμα and the genitive σώματος. Other neuters lose a stem-final τ in the same way: φῶς has the genitive φωτός and ὕδωρ the genitive ὕδατος.

Stems in -ν (αἰών, ποιμήν) keep the ν, and it falls away before -σι: αἰῶσιν. Stems in -ντ (ἄρχων) show it in the genitive, ἄρχοντος. You will not be asked to derive these changes; you will be asked to recognise a form and to go from the genitive to the stem.

sections.heading: Gender is not given by the ending
body: The ending of a third-declension noun does not tell you its gender as reliably as the endings of the first and second declensions do. The article does. Nouns in -μα are neuter, and many in -ις (χάρις, ἐλπίς) are feminine, but you should learn the gender with the noun, together with its article: ἡ σάρξ, τὸ πνεῦμα, ὁ ἄρχων.

misunderstandings: The nominative singular is not the stem. The stem of σάρξ is σαρκ-, of ὄνομα it is ὀνοματ-, and of χάρις it is χαριτ-. Always take it from the genitive.
The nominative and accusative of a neuter are alike, in the singular (πνεῦμα) and in the plural (ὀνόματα). The article and the verb show which is meant. This is not special to the third declension.
In the dative plural the stem-final consonant may have dropped out before -σι(ν), as in ποσίν, from ποδ-. Do not expect to see the whole stem there; check the genitive.

deeper.heading: Why the third declension looks so irregular
body: The third declension collects all the nouns whose stems end in a consonant, and each stem-final consonant behaves a little differently. Grammarians group them by that consonant. The variety is mostly the result of ordinary sound changes that apply to a consonant when it stands next to σ or at the end of a word. Once you know those changes, the forms are far less arbitrary than the first lists make them look.

examples.analysis: σαρκὸς is the genitive singular of σάρξ, and its stem is σαρκ-; σάρξ is the nominative, the predicate of ἐστιν. πνεύματος and πνεῦμα are the genitive and the nominative of the neuter πνεῦμα: the stem πνευματ- shows in the genitive and has lost its final consonant in the nominative. The two halves of the verse are built alike, so the forms can be compared directly.
